home.title: goflag — the site problems humans can’t catch at scale
home.description: A CLI that reports broken links, missing translation pages, a robots.txt that contradicts your pages, and misconfigured SEO metadata. JSON-first, MIT.

changelog.title: Changelog
changelog.description: Every published version of @goflag/cli, generated from the commit history, with the release notes that explain what a version actually changes.

hero.eyebrow: MIT · Node {node} · no account, no dashboard
hero.title: Nobody can check 400 pages by hand.
hero.lead: A hreflang pointing at a 404. A canonical that quietly de-indexed a page. A robots.txt that contradicts every meta tag on the site. goflag crawls once, judges what it found, and hands you a JSON report you can gate CI on.
hero.expectRed: Expect it to be red. Almost every site that has never been audited carries a backlog — that is not a reason to wait until it is clean.

checks.title: Four things, checked properly
checks.lead: Deliberately small. No dashboard, no config system, no social-preview gallery — just the findings, as a report you can pipe, diff or gate on.

links.title: Broken links
links.body: Every link on every crawled page, deduplicated globally so a footer link on 500 pages is probed once. HEAD then GET, redirect chains and loops, soft 404s, and anti-bot 403s triaged apart from real breakage.
links.detail: Mapped back to the pages that reference them.

translations.title: Missing translation pages
translations.body: A route × locale matrix seeded from your sitemap, not only from links — a site with no hreflang gives a link crawler nothing to follow into its other locales. Plus reciprocity gaps, missing x-default and invalid locale tags.
translations.detail: Deliberate gaps are declared, not tolerated.

robots.title: robots.txt policy
robots.body: A site that forbids crawling while its pages ask to be indexed. Both declarations cannot hold, robots.txt wins, and so the meta tag is never even read.
robots.detail: A warning on staging, an error in production.

metadata.title: SEO metadata
metadata.body: Eleven checks on the head of every page: title and description presence and length, canonical presence and absoluteness, og:title, og:description, og:image, viewport, and contradictory robots directives.
metadata.detail: Each finding carries an App Router fix.

terminal.title: The whole interface
terminal.lead: There is no UI to show you. The terminal output is a render of the JSON report, and the JSON is the source of truth.
terminal.caption: Real output, reformatted for the page. Progress goes to stderr so stdout stays clean for the report.

invisible.title: What a browser cannot show you
invisible.lead: Each of these renders perfectly. The defect is in the part of the page nobody looks at, and the cost is paid in a search index you never see.

one.see: A page that renders exactly as designed.
one.consequence: The page asks to be dropped in favour of another. It will be.

two.see: Four locales, every one of them reachable.
two.consequence: Each translation competes with the other three instead of consolidating with them.

three.see: A live production site, serving traffic.
three.consequence: No page is ever fetched, so the index directive on every page is never read.

method.title: Gate on regressions, not on perfection
method.lead: A run that fails on any finding is unusable on a site that is not clean yet — so it gets switched off, or quietly ignored. Three flags make the gate tenable, and one of them makes the backlog actually shrink.

step1.title: Capture a baseline
step1.body: Freeze today’s findings as known, so the gate can ask whether this change made things worse instead of whether the site is perfect. It prints how many it grandfathered and the ceiling to set next. Commit the file.

step2.title: Gate on what is new
step2.body: Findings are matched by fingerprint, and page URLs are normalised to origin-independent routes — so a baseline captured against production compares cleanly with a run against localhost.

step3.title: Lower the ratchet
step3.body: Fix a finding, drop --max-debt by one, commit both. This is the only part that makes the backlog shrink; without it a baseline fossilises behind a build that passes.

method.honestyTitle: This mode passes builds on sites with known defects
method.honestyBody: That is what it is for, and why it has to be asked for by name — --baseline on its own is an error. The output never says clean and never goes green while findings are outstanding. It says how many are being let through, and how old the baseline is.

ci.title: In CI
ci.lead: Two moments are worth auditing, and they answer different questions. Neither replaces the other: only the deployed run sees what the environment injects.
ci.mrAgainst: The branch’s own build, booted by --start
ci.deployAnswers: Is what is actually serving correct?
ci.flagsBody: --static needs no browser, so the job runs on a plain Node image and cannot be slowed by a Chromium download. --no-external skips off-origin links, which are the ones you cannot fix and whose failures are somebody else’s outage — a gate that goes red because a third party is down teaches people to ignore it. Audit external links on a schedule, where nobody is waiting.
ci.pinBody: A floating version turns somebody else’s release into a red pipeline on a commit that touched nothing, and the job is only worth having if red means you broke something.

proof.title: Built by auditing my own sites
proof.lead: There is no logo wall here, because there are no logos. goflag exists because four sites I run needed it, and every number below is measured rather than estimated.
proof.storyTitle: The bug it was built to fix was its own
proof.storyBody: The first version reported zero missing translations on a four-locale site that carried not a single hreflang tag. The locale axis was derived from the alternates the pages declared — so a silent site had exactly one column, and every check passed vacuously.
proof.storyPunch: goflag was detecting the absence of hreflang by reading the hreflang.
proof.fpTitle: Five false positives, published rather than buried
proof.fpBody: Capturing the first baselines surfaced five ways the tool was wrong. The worst read the path segment /cv as Chuvash — a real ISO 639-1 code — and invented 31 translation holes that never existed. Another stripped a trailing slash before probing a link and declared 159 working citations dead, which sent someone to fix content that was already correct.
proof.fpPunch: They are fixed, and they are why goflag now refuses to guess a locale axis at all: with no sitemap and no --locales, it reports the prefixes it saw with the evidence for each, and turns the i18n checks off.

not.title: What goflag is not
not.lead: Knowing quickly that this is the wrong tool is worth more to you than a long evaluation.

items.dashboard: No hosted dashboard, and nothing to log into
items.account: No account, no API key, no seat
items.rank: No rank tracking and no keyword research
items.vitals: No Core Web Vitals, no Lighthouse score
items.telemetry: No telemetry — nothing leaves your machine but requests to the site you named

not.closing: One command, a JSON report, an exit code. If what you want is a number to optimise, this is the wrong tool: a score invites optimising the score.

rules.title: The rule catalogue
rules.lead: Eleven per-page rules and three site-wide ones. Every finding names the rule that produced it, so a report can be argued with.
rules.honestyTitle: The length thresholds are heuristics, and are labelled as such
rules.honestyBody: Nothing in the catalogue yet cites a specification. Phase 3 of the plan gives every rule a rigor level and a dated source; until that lands, treat the title and description windows as the conventions they are rather than as anything normative.

faq.title: Questions worth answering before you install

source.q: Does it need access to my source code?
source.a: No. It needs a URL. goflag reads what a crawler reads, which is also why it catches things a local build cannot show you — the real base URL, whatever the proxy serves for robots.txt, the redirects.

next.a: The checks do: they judge HTML, and HTML is HTML. The fix snippets attached to findings assume the Next.js App Router, and say so. Nothing breaks on a Rails or Astro site; you just get the finding without the copy-paste remedy.

chromium.a: Only without --static. By default, a page whose head looks empty — no title, no description, no canonical, no Open Graph, no JSON-LD — is re-rendered in headless Chromium so a client-rendered app is not reported as missing everything. --static turns that off, including the detection, and never downloads a browser. playwright is an optional peer dependency, so nothing is installed unless you ask.

privacy.a: The HTTP requests to the site you named, and nothing else. No telemetry, no account, no upload. The report is written to your disk or your stdout.

zerox.a: Because the API will still move. It was extracted from four sites I run rather than designed in the abstract, and pretending otherwise would be the kind of claim this tool exists to catch.

scale.q: Will it finish on a large site?
scale.a: The largest site it gates is {pages} pages and takes about {duration} with --static --no-external. --max-pages caps the crawl, --include and --exclude narrow it, and a run that hit a cap says so in diagnostics rather than reporting a smaller number as if it were the whole site.

close.title: Point it at your site.
close.lead: One command, no install, nothing to sign up for. Then read the five steps that take you from a red first run to a gate you trust.

notFound.lead: This page does not exist. If a link on this site brought you here, that is a broken link — and there is a tool for that.
notFound.irony: Yes, the irony is noted. The site is audited by goflag in its own pipeline; a 404 reachable from a link would fail that build.
